video_title: The AI Bubble Didn’t Pop. Hedge Fund Leverage Did.
gist: Jordi Visser argues the sell-off in AI stocks is a hedge fund leverage unwind (Vara, Lone Pine, record prime-broker leverage, credit and converts weakness), not an AI bubble burst, citing sold-out compute, rising GPU prices and fast lab revenue growth. He frames LTCM-style leverage lessons, stays long AI compute and crypto, and warns pain could last into hyperscaler earnings and the midterms.

themes.theme: Hedge fund deleveraging, not an AI bubble

insights.claim: The thing that popped in the week before this video was hedge fund leverage, not an equity or AI bubble: the S&P 500 was only about 2.7% off its all-time high while the AI trade, crowded in hedge fund books, sold off hard.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Dips in AI stocks are positioning-driven, so they may be buyable rather than the start of a 2000/2008-style crash.
insights.quote: There is a bubble being popped. It is not in the equity market, and it is not in the economy.

insights.claim: Hedge fund leverage is in a dismantling and will not exceed its recent peak again, because the market-structure change makes it hard to produce a sensible Sharpe ratio at high leverage.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect structurally lower gross leverage and less liquidity support for crowded momentum names.

insights.claim: Hedge fund leverage per Fed and OFR data was roughly flat from 2018 to 2023 and then more than doubled to record highs through Q1; prime-broker and broker-dealer financing grew about 15%, with long/short equity near 2:1 gross.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The unwind has a large stock of leverage to work through, so it could take a while.
insights.quote: The hedge fund industry is at all-time record leverage.

insights.claim: Hedge funds cannot hold drawdowns because most do not have five-year locked capital; month-to-month benchmarks and drawdown limits force them to cut risk together, and the AI winners-versus-losers pair trade is on in nearly every book.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Forced, correlated selling can hit even stocks whose fundamentals are improving.

insights.claim: Goldman's crowded hedge fund long basket, which is market neutral and unlevered, fell about 10% in July and then dropped in a straight line through the month discussed, a post-Lehman-sized move; with leverage the fund-level losses would be much larger.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fund-level pain is far greater than the unlevered basket suggests, so more liquidation is plausible.

insights.claim: Named hedge fund casualties: Vara's roughly $20B AI flagship fell 44% in one month, wiping out a 65% year-to-date gain, and Lone Pine gave up a 44% gain in a quarter, which Visser estimates is over 55% gross, a GFC-sized drawdown for a top fund.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Short-stacked funds will not add risk, which removes marginal buyers.
insights.quote: This is LTCM-ish. That's what it is.

insights.claim: The pain trade is for hedge funds to stay risk-off through hyperscaler earnings and possibly the midterm elections, with a snapback at year-end if this is only a positioning shakeout and not a bubble.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Timing of the bottom is uncertain, so staged entries beat a single bet on the low.

insights.claim: Visser says he does not know when the hedge fund pain ends given roughly $14 trillion of positioning, and it could take another month or more even if fundamentals stay strong.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Being early on a rebound is likely even if the thesis is right.

insights.claim: The unwind spread beyond equities in the week discussed: HYG versus IEF (a synthetic credit carry trade) gave back its summer gains, and the convertible bond index sold off in a waterfall after July's reluctant dip. Visser says credit stress is when multi-strat pods really get hurt because it hits many strategies at once.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Watch credit and converts as the signal of whether this escalates beyond an equity positioning event.

insights.claim: Huge AI capital raises (Broadcom and Google each over $100B this year, plus SpaceX, Anthropic and OpenAI) force investors to sell other assets such as Treasuries and equities to fund them, which pressures markets broadly.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The near-term risk is capital supply for AI, not demand, so supply of new issuance is a headwind.

themes.theme: Market structure and Nvidia multiple compression

insights.claim: Nvidia's stock is roughly flat over a year despite earnings blowing away consensus, so its forward P/E has fallen to about 15 (closer to 10 on higher estimates); this stopped rewarding hedge funds' information edge and spread across the AI trade.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Earnings beats no longer produce stock gains, which breaks the hedge fund model of trading on better information.

insights.claim: Visser argues terminal value has been destroyed: no one can know whether any company's earnings beyond about three years will exist, so the Q1-style melt-up will not return in public stocks.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Public equity returns get capped relative to private tokenized and AI exponential assets.
insights.quote: You will never go through what you went through in the first quarter again, ever again in public stocks, ever.

insights.claim: Single-name volatility has exploded while index volatility barely moved (VIX near 20), so there is no cheap hedge for the AI trade, which spans sectors; there is no S&P put that hedges it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Hedged books are unprotected, adding to forced selling.

insights.claim: Hedge fund competition on speed to ideas is gone because anyone can use AI to screen 100 names down to 15 with fundamentals, technicals and thematic research in seconds, which is another reason hedge fund market structure is changing.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Informational edge for institutions is eroding, so leverage and fees are harder to justify.

insights.claim: Money may aggregate into larger hedge funds with a risk-management advantage, and returns can stay similar with less leverage, but the industry-wide Sharpe will be harder to deliver.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect consolidation toward the biggest platforms.

insights.claim: Correlations are breaking: the Mexican Bolsa was near 52-week lows in the same stretch that the QQQ was weak, and fertilizer, crop inputs and software shorts were also moving violently, which shows the deleveraging is cross-sector.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Pair and diversification hedges stop working during forced deleveraging.

insights.claim: The week's S&P drawdown was small versus GFC (almost 60%), dot-com (50%) and COVID (near 40%); the S&P was only 2.7% off its high and up about 12% year to date, so the bubble-pop narrative does not fit the price data.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Check rolling drawdowns before accepting crash narratives.

insights.claim: In 2007 the housing bubble showed defaults and wide credit spreads long before equities fell; today there are no AI payment defaults, no earnings misses and no GPU price declines, so it is not the same setup.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Credit spreads are the better tell, and they have not signaled a bubble pop.

insights.claim: The dot-com bust was a supply build funded by leveraged fiber companies with no demand, whereas AI today has demand outrunning supply, and the fiber buildout ran about seven years while AI is only in year two.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Calling the top in year two of a buildout has the wrong shape versus history.

insights.claim: LTCM lessons from leverage: the thesis can be right but timing, volatility, financing, crowding, correlation breaks, liquidity and position sizing can wipe out the levered holder; Nvidia could be up 300% next year and the fund still be gone.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Apply these seven risk lenses to any crowded levered AI position.
insights.quote: Your fundamental thesis can be correct. But, the timing.

themes.theme: AI demand, capex and revenue growth

insights.claim: Anthropic is on pace for roughly $90-100B revenue this year after finishing last year at about $9B, having grown about 10x in each of the past years; OpenAI and Anthropic combined are around $170B this year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Revenue is compounding faster than bear models assume.

insights.claim: A cited analyst view that AI capex could reach about $2T or 5-6% of GDP next year, with OpenAI plus Anthropic reaching $600-700B revenue, implies roughly a 3x from their current combined level, which Visser calls a built-in deceleration versus their 10x history.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Consensus-type revenue paths already embed sharp slowdowns, so upside surprise is plausible.

insights.claim: Bearish long-range forecasts out to 2030-2031 (Gartner on $3.5T of AI infrastructure impairment, Bain on an $800B funding shortfall, a Barclays desk note) are guesses with no facts behind them; Visser has never seen forecasts out to 2030 matter and says the same shops missed Micron's rise.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fade headline-grabbing long-dated bearish forecasts; they are poor trading signals.
insights.quote: I've never in my history of trading markets seen a forecast out to 2030 that anyone cared about.

insights.claim: Hard supply-side contracts contradict the bubble story: Micron says signed agreements cover over 35% of its revenue through 2030, ASML sees AI chip demand into 2030 and shortages through 2028, Lumentum is sold out of AI parts until 2029, Amazon's Andy Jassy says AI compute is sold out beyond 2028, and Nvidia guided about 70% revenue growth.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Demand visibility into 2028-2030 is documented, unlike the bears' forecasts.

insights.claim: GPU prices, including old H100s, are higher than a year ago, and DRAM prices made new highs, so a GPU glut bear case or a bubble burst is hard to argue; one can only be bearish on CoreWeave's equity or bonds specifically.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Compute scarcity supports neocloud collateral value.

insights.claim: Revenue pools for frontier AI may come from robotics, biotech, nanotech and materials, drug discovery and chip design, not just chatbot subscriptions and token APIs, and that revenue has not started yet; analysts extrapolating linearly miss this.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Top-down revenue models that only count current products understate the pool.

insights.claim: Agent adoption is just beginning: over 50% of companies use coding agents but only about 2% use agent workflows, and agent swarms and consumer agents appeared only in the last couple of months, which Visser frames as a step-up in demand for compute.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Workflow agents are the next wave of token demand and of white-collar job pressure.

insights.claim: Brad Gerstner's framing, which Visser endorses: frontier labs are only about a third of AI compute demand, there is roughly $500B a year of classical compute replacement, and Jensen Huang answers the question of how long the buildout lasts with 'forever', making this a permanent re-architecture of compute, not a visible-end capex cycle.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The bear case treats a structural shift as a cycle.

insights.claim: OpenAI/Anthropic valuations of about $1.5-2T mean that even if they stay flat from here they have already won, since they were under $100B (Anthropic under $5B) two years earlier.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Judging them on whether they reach $10T misses the return already earned.

insights.claim: The Mag 7 emerged from the iPhone era unpredictably, and AI will produce a similar set of dominant winners that nobody can forecast ex ante; Visser does not think they will necessarily be OpenAI and Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Exposure should be diversified across the AI stack.

insights.claim: SemiAnalysis, which Visser calls the best AI research shop, grew revenue from about $20M in 2025 to $100M with 90 employees, and its AI spend rose from about $100K a year ago to $10-11M by August, as an example of AI-native firms scaling faster than public companies can.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: AI-native private firms capture growth that public markets cannot access.

insights.claim: Visser recommends AI agent and Vera Rubin related names for the next 12 months, with a list of 15, mostly optical, bought into the weakness; he still holds Marvell, some Micron, Nvidia and Eli Lilly, but his AI portfolio is well down and will never be as large as crypto again.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: He is leaning on optical and agentic compute names while cutting overall AI size.

insights.claim: Semis (SMH) are still up about 50% year to date despite the panics, and in seven of the last eight years semis returned 40% or more; ignoring semis is ignoring the Mag 7 equivalent.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: The drawdown is happening inside a strong trend.

insights.claim: Visser prefers CoreWeave's bonds to its equity, believing that if revenues come in people will prefer its debt to Treasuries; its clients (Microsoft, OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic, Mistral, Jane Street) are strong, so a default is not a near-term risk, though the equity can carry a higher risk premium.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Capital structure choice: debt over equity in the neocloud complex.
insights.quote: I'd rather have the debt at this point at these levels.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler stocks (Amazon, Meta, Google, Microsoft) made new all-time highs as a group, which contradicts the claim that capital markets are shutting off AI funding.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler strength is a check on the bubble narrative.

insights.claim: Bitcoin was down only about 2.3% in the week the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, and the crypto index is down about 7% month to date; Visser holds the majority of his portfolio in crypto and expects Bitcoin may not rise until hedge fund stabilization, possibly drifting toward 75.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Crypto is showing relative strength, but upside is likely gated by the hedge fund unwind.

insights.claim: Tokenization is the final stage of hedge fund deleveraging: it will change covariance matrices and how margin is provided, and Visser sees returns in the tokenized digital economy dwarfing public equities, private equity, private credit, VC and bonds.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A long-dated bet on market-structure disruption to traditional asset classes.

insights.claim: AI agents will bring the demand crypto lacked, comparable to the end of the dot-com bubble for crypto, which is why Visser holds crypto positions.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Agent-driven transaction demand is his crypto thesis.

themes.theme: Macro: jobs, confidence and equity compounding

insights.claim: Consumer confidence hit its lowest level since 2013, below pandemic levels, driven by labor-market perceptions; the jobs-hard-to-get versus plentiful gap implies an unemployment rate nearer 6% than the current level.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Official jobs data may understate weakness, which matters into the midterms.

insights.claim: Financial and tech payrolls have been shrinking, and with the exception of health care the rest of the labor market has been negative for around 18 months; agent workflows could add a profit-margin and political effect more than a recession.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect labor-market weakness paired with high margins, which can influence Fed and political responses.

insights.claim: S&P 500 earnings growth is about 29% year over year, and compounding over 10/20/30/40 years has given 17%/13%/12%/13% annualized, so $10 a month for 50 years would be about $478,000.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Long-term compounding argues against reacting to weekly noise.

insights.claim: Crypto-related net interest income cited at up to $107B next year would, according to Visser, be money coming out of the traditional system (referencing Stripe versus Citibank).
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Fintech and stablecoin interest income is a flow shift worth tracking.
